entries.title: Protein powders as a category
entries.result: Clean Label Project says it tested 165 top-selling protein powders and analyzed data on 160 products from 70 brands. It reports that 47% exceeded at least one federal or state limit, including California's Prop 65, and 21% were over twice the Prop 65 lead level. Plant-based powders generally had the highest contaminant levels, and chocolate powders had 110 times more cadmium than vanilla.
entries.threshold: Federal and state limits, including California Prop 65.
caveats: This describes the category, not the product in front of you.
Results depend on the products and thresholds the tester chose.

source.label: Clean Label Project, protein powder study (2025)

entries.ties: Clean Label Project is a nonprofit (501(c)(3)) that is not required to disclose its donors. In 2020 trade press reported industry critics accusing it of profiting from products it certifies and of unclear methods; its director said its product-ratings data licensing ended and described Amazon charity donations and small individual gifts. It launched a code-of-practice certification in October 2019. Its funding for this study was not found.

entries.title: Packaged baby foods as a category
entries.result: Consumer Reports tested 48 baby foods from 11 brands. 96% had heavy metals below its level of concern. Inorganic arsenic was detected in 77%, cadmium in 80% and lead in 85%. Phthalates were found in 81%. Of 16 products tested for microplastics, it found strong evidence of microplastic particles in each of the 15 purées.
entries.threshold: Consumer Reports' level of concern, based on the strictest health-based limits it could find.
caveats: This describes the category, not the product in front of you.
Consumer Reports says microplastics have no regulatory limits and their health effects are still being studied.

entries.response: The U.S. Rice Federation said the industry has studied arsenic uptake for more than a decade. Walmart and Whole Foods Market gave statements about their testing and standards. Ten companies did not respond, including Mahatma, Goya and Rice-A-Roni.
entries.check: Source check: figures and company responses compared with the source page on 2026-10-04
entries.title: Rice and rice products as a category
entries.result: CR tested 52 rice products (142 samples) and found inorganic arsenic in all of them. Seventeen averaged 100 ppb or more. Category averages ranged from 55 ppb (basmati) to 113 ppb (brown rice). Three of six rice mixes had more than 0.5 micrograms of lead a serving, mostly from the spice mix. CR advises, from its older 2014 tests, a maximum of about 2.75 servings a week for adults for most rice and 5 for white basmati or sushi rice.
entries.threshold: There is no federal arsenic limit for rice. CR used the FDA's 100 parts per billion action level for infant rice cereal as a reference mark, and its own 0.5 micrograms of lead a day level of concern. It also used a cancer-risk method that the EPA uses to set weekly serving advice.
entries.serving: 1/4 cup dry rice, or 1 cup cooked pouch rice
caveats: This describes the category, not the product in front of you.
